questions.question: What is the core goal of Private Set Intersection (PSI)?
options: Let two parties learn the exact union A ∪ B
Let one or both parties learn (something about) A ∩ B without revealing the rest of the sets
Let two parties compute a shared secret key for encryption
Let a server prove it knows its entire dataset to a client
questions.explanation: PSI is about learning the intersection while minimizing what each side learns about the non-intersecting elements.

questions.question: In a commutative-encryption PSI sketch using exponentiation mod p, what does 'commutative' mean?
options: Enc_a(Enc_b(m)) equals Enc_b(Enc_a(m)) for all messages
Enc_a(m) can be decrypted without knowing a
Enc_a(m) is constant-time for all inputs
Enc_a(m) is secure even when p is small
questions.explanation: Commutativity means applying party A's transform then party B's transform yields the same result as doing them in the opposite order.

questions.question: Why must the client's exponent a be coprime with (p−1) in the exponentiation-based PSI demo?
options: So that a has an inverse modulo (p−1), enabling unblinding
So that a is smaller than p and fits in 64 bits
So that the server cannot shuffle the response
So that SHA-256 outputs are uniformly random
questions.explanation: Unblinding requires computing inv(a) mod (p−1); that inverse exists exactly when gcd(a, p−1)=1.

questions.question: What changes when the server sorts (or otherwise reorders) the client's re-encrypted items before returning them?
options: The client can still learn which of its items are in the intersection
The client can only learn an unordered intersection size (not item-by-item membership) unless extra structure is used
The protocol becomes information-theoretically secure
The server learns the client's plaintext items
questions.explanation: Reordering breaks per-item alignment, so the client can only compare sets (cardinality) rather than map matches back to specific items.

questions.question: Which piece of information typically leaks in basic PSI protocols even if the intersection stays private?
options: The exact non-intersection elements
The private keys a and b
The set sizes (|A| and |B|), and often timing/traffic shape
A proof that all elements are prime numbers
questions.explanation: Most PSI designs leak at least set sizes and some metadata unless you add padding/batching and traffic-shaping.

questions.question: A Bloom filter is used as a membership structure for server tags. What does a 'match' mean?
options: The element is definitely in the server set (no error possible)
The element is definitely not in the server set
The element is possibly in the server set (false positives are possible)
The server's secret key can be recovered
questions.explanation: Bloom filters have no false negatives for inserted items, but they can produce false positives for non-members.

questions.question: If the item domain is small (e.g., phone numbers) and you run PSI repeatedly, what is a common mitigation to reduce offline guessing and linkability?
options: Use a smaller prime p so computations run faster
Use an OPRF/VOPRF-style protocol so tags are keyed and hard to enumerate without the key
Replace SHA-256 with CRC32 so hashes are shorter
Disable shuffling so the client can map responses to items
questions.explanation: An OPRF/VOPRF makes it harder for attackers to precompute tags over a small domain and reduces cross-run linkability when designed with key rotation.

questions.question: Which abuse risk exists when a client is allowed to run 'reveal intersection' PSI without restrictions?
options: The client can turn PSI into a membership oracle by querying one candidate at a time
The client can force the server to reveal its secret exponent b directly
The client can bypass TLS and sniff plaintext packets
The client can compute discrete logs in any group instantly
questions.explanation: A malicious client can query many candidates and learn whether the server contains each one, so real systems enforce authorization and rate limits.
